title: The Lesson I Learned From Lazarus' Tomb
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From Lazarus' Tomb
Not the peaceful kind of silence people write about in greeting cards. Not the silence of rest.
The kind that settles over dreams that never happened, prayers that seemed unanswered, relationships that died, opportunities that vanished, and hopes buried beneath stone.
Most of us know that silence.
We know what it feels like to stand before something we loved and whisper, “God, where were You?”
That is why the story of Lazarus reaches so deeply into the human soul.
Because before it is a story about resurrection, it is a story about disappointment.
Before it is a story about life, it is a story about grief.
Before it is a story about glory, it is a story about a tomb.
And perhaps that is exactly where many of us are standing right now.
Not necessarily one made of stone.
One built from years of waiting.
One built from the crushing feeling that God arrived too late.
Lazarus, whose name comes from the Hebrew אלעזר (Elʿazar), means “God has helped.”
The man named “God has helped” is dying.
His sisters, Mary and Martha, send word to Jesus.
“Lord, behold, he whom You love is sick.”
Notice what they did not say.
They simply appealed to His love.
Because surely if Jesus loved Lazarus, He would come immediately.
Surely He would stop the tragedy.
Surely He would prevent the funeral.
But Jesus does something that still confuses believers today.
“So, when He heard that Lazarus was sick, He stayed two more days in the place where He was.”
Many people have abandoned their faith because God did not move according to their timetable.
But Scripture repeatedly teaches that God's delays are not God's denials.
His timing is not our timing.
His perspective is not our perspective.
What looked like neglect was actually preparation.
What looked like abandonment was actually divine orchestration.
He was preparing a greater revelation of His glory.
And perhaps that is a lesson many of us desperately need.
Because sometimes God allows situations to move beyond human solutions.
Not because He has forgotten us.
But because He intends to reveal Himself in a way we would never experience otherwise.
By the time Jesus arrives, Lazarus is dead.
In Jewish understanding, four days removed all possibility of misunderstanding.
No one could claim Lazarus merely fainted.
No one could claim he was unconscious.
No one could claim a medical error.
Martha meets Jesus and says words that countless believers have spoken in different forms throughout history:
“Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” (John 11:21)
Can you hear the question hidden beneath the statement?
Many followers of Christ have carried these questions.
Yet Jesus responds with a declaration that changes everything.
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή.
Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē.
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
Notice what He does not say.
He does not say resurrection is coming.
He does not merely say He can perform resurrection.
Life itself is standing before the tomb.
Hope itself is standing before despair.
The Creator is standing before death.
The One who spoke galaxies into existence is standing before a grave.
The shortest verse in the English Bible becomes one of the deepest revelations of God's heart.
The Son of God knew Lazarus would walk out alive.
He knew resurrection was minutes away.
He knew the miracle was coming.
Because divine power does not eliminate divine compassion.
Jesus was not detached from human suffering.
The God of Scripture is not indifferent to your pain.
He is not distant from your tears.
He is not unmoved by your grief.
The Savior who raises the dead is also the Savior who cries beside mourners.
“Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.” (John 11:39)
How many people have said the same thing about their lives?
Yet impossible situations are often the stage upon which God displays His greatest glory.
The stone was not Jesus' responsibility.
There are stones many people are still holding in place.
And God is saying the same thing today.
Then comes one of the most powerful commands ever spoken.
The voice that called creation from nothing now calls life from death.
The grave clothes remain, but death no longer owns him.
And there, standing before the tomb, I learned something I will never forget.
The greatest miracle in the story is not merely that Lazarus walked out.
It is that Jesus walked in.
Because that is what Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Humanity's story was headed toward eternal death.
At the cross He carried our sin.
At the resurrection He defeated death.
And through faith He offers eternal life.
The lesson from Lazarus' tomb is not simply that Jesus can resurrect dead things.
The lesson is that He specializes in situations everyone else has given up on.
The person reading this who secretly wonders if God can still use them.
The answer from Bethany is yes.
Because Jesus has never been intimidated by a tomb.
If He can call Lazarus out of a grave after four days, He can call purpose out of your failure.
He can call hope out of your despair.
He can call healing out of your wounds.
He can call redemption out of your scandal.
He can call life out of what everyone else believes is dead.
That is why we continue telling these stories.
But to point people toward the Savior who still transforms lives today.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.

Many readers have found that surrounding themselves with biblical truth daily strengthens their walk with Christ. Supporting this ministry is one practical way to help spread biblical truth and glorify God through Gospel-centered content that changes lives.
Follow for daily biblical encouragement, discipleship, truth, healing, and Gospel-centered content.
Because the same Jesus who stood outside Lazarus' tomb is still calling people from death to life today.
And perhaps the stone you thought marked the end of your story is actually the place where God is preparing His greatest revelation.
The tomb was never the final chapter.
